The Mahler Conjecture for General Convex Bodies
Symplectic Balls in Symmetric Polar Products

evidence.note: Lean proofs of the symmetric bound and its equality cases, the general simplex bound and the symplectic width 4, each with a Comparator statement. The functional inequalities are not formalized.

headline: Symmetric convex bodies cannot beat Mahler's volume bound.
scope: The headline bound needs origin symmetry. The companion general-body paper drops it, with the smaller simplex constant. The symplectic paper still assumes symmetry.
plain: Every symmetric convex body (a solid centered on the origin) has a polar body. The polar is the set of points y with x·y ≤ 1 for every point x of the body. The paper proves that the volume product, the body's volume times its polar's volume, never drops below 4^n/n!. Only linear images of Hanner polytopes (cube-like shapes built from intervals) reach this floor, and the paper also derives a sharp functional form. Companion papers prove the nonsymmetric version (simplices are the minimizers) and a symplectic width of 4 for K × K° when n ≥ 2.
doesNot: This does not compute the volume product of any specific body.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proofs hold, they settle an 87-year-old central problem in convex geometry.

sections.title: The story
sections.body: In 1939, Kurt Mahler asked how small the volume product of a symmetric convex body and its polar could be. He proved the planar case himself. In 1956, Olof Hanner built the cube-like shapes that later became the conjectured minimizers. In 1981, Jean Saint-Raymond proved the sharp bound for unconditional bodies (those symmetric under sign flips of coordinates). In 1985 and 1986, Shlomo Reisner proved the sharp bound for zonoids. In 1987, Jean Bourgain and Vitali Milman proved a dimension-free exponential lower bound. In 2008, Greg Kuperberg made that bound explicit and stronger with Gauss linking integrals. In 2014, Shiri Artstein-Avidan, Roman Karasev and Yaron Ostrover linked the problem to symplectic capacity. In 2020, Hiroshi Iriyeh and Masataka Shibata settled the three-dimensional symmetric case with equality. In 2022, Fradelizi, Hubard, Meyer, Roldán-Pensado and Zvavitch gave a shorter proof of that case, with stability. For general bodies, Mathieu Meyer and Reisner (2006) and Jaegil Kim and Reisner (2011) gave partial results. In 2026, Shibing Chen, Yuanyuan Li, Dongmeng Xi and Zhe-Feng Xu solved the general three-dimensional case. These papers prove the bound in every dimension and classify all equality cases.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.body: The volume product is unchanged by linear maps, so the bound is a universal law of shape, not an accident of coordinates. Equality goes exactly to linear Hanner bodies, and the companion nonsymmetric bound crowns the simplex.

sections.title: Where it leads
sections.body: A companion paper proves a stronger statement for n ≥ 2. The product of any symmetric body with its polar, K × K°, has Gromov width 4. That fact by itself implies the symmetric volume bound. The papers also derive sharp functional versions. Stability, meaning how close near-minimizers are to Hanner bodies, is a possible next step that the papers do not claim.

sections.title: What it says about AI
sections.body: The manuscripts list OpenAI as author, and the repository states that an internal model produced them. The reasoning summary covers three separate attempts: the symmetric bound, its equality cases and the general case. It shows the model testing routes from Kuperberg's linking integrals to Klartag's covariance framework. The Lean scope note describes formal proofs of four results. They are the symmetric bound, its equality cases, the general simplex bound and the symplectic width 4. Each has a Comparator statement. The functional inequalities are not formalized, and an embedding at capacity exactly 4 is not asserted.

hypeCheck: The main geometric statements have Lean formal proofs that can be checked with Comparator. The functional corollaries do not, and the repository reports no independent expert review.

glossary.meaning: A solid shape with no dents and a well-defined volume.
The set of points y with x·y ≤ 1 for every point x of the body; a bigger body has a smaller polar.
A body's volume times its polar's volume, unchanged by linear maps.
A cube-like shape built from intervals by products and joins.
The simplest closed shape in its dimension, like a triangle or tetrahedron.
An inequality about functions instead of shapes.
The largest ball that fits inside a symplectic shape.

claims.text: Every origin-symmetric convex body satisfies |K||K°| ≥ 4^n/n!, with equality exactly for linear Hanner bodies.
claims.sourceLine: For every integer … and every origin-symmetric convex body … Equality holds if and only if K is a linear Hanner body.

claims.text: Mahler posed the volume-product problem in 1939.
claims.sourceLine: Mahler introduced the volume-product problem in his work on convex bodies and transference in the geometry of numbers [Mahler1939].

claims.text: Saint-Raymond proved the sharp bound for unconditional bodies.
claims.sourceLine: Saint-Raymond proved the sharp inequality for unconditional bodies (those invariant under coordinate sign changes) [SaintRaymond1981]; Meyer and Reisner identified the Hanner equality cases in that class [Meyer1986,Reisner1987].

claims.text: Bourgain and Milman gave an exponential bound; Kuperberg made it explicit and stronger.
claims.sourceLine: Bourgain and Milman established such a reverse Blaschke--Santaló inequality [BourgainMilman]; Kuperberg obtained an explicit stronger bound by a geometric argument using Gauss linking integrals [Kuperberg].

claims.text: Iriyeh and Shibata proved the three-dimensional symmetric theorem with equality.
claims.sourceLine: Iriyeh and Shibata proved the complete three-dimensional symmetric theorem, including equality [Theorem 1.1][IriyehShibata].

claims.text: Chen, Li, Xi and Xu treated the nonsymmetric three-dimensional problem in a 2026 preprint.
claims.sourceLine: Chen, Li, Xi, and Xu recently gave a shadow-flow proof of that theorem in a preprint that also treats the nonsymmetric three-dimensional problem [Theorem 7.1][ChenLiXiXu2026].

claims.text: The release overview states sharp functional Mahler inequalities and, for n ≥ 2, Gromov width 4 for symmetric polar products.
claims.sourceLine: The corresponding sharp functional Mahler inequalities also hold. For n ≥ 2, every symmetric polar product … in dimension … has Gromov width 4.

claims.text: Gromov width 4 for K × K° implies the symmetric Mahler bound; equality cases are not claimed there.
claims.sourceLine: Thus the theorem resolves the symmetric Mahler conjecture positively; the complete deduction, including the one-dimensional case, appears in Corollary~\ref{cor:mahler}. We make no claim here about the classification of equality cases.
